documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: Generative AI Policy for Students (August 2023)
documents.stance_why: The policy says use 'in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member' is an Honor Code violation, so AI is off unless the instructor allows it, while it also praises supportive uses. That is restrict rather than delegates, because it fixes a default.
documents.summary: The university-wide student policy from the Office of Academic Standards. It praises AI for brainstorming, study aids and concept help but frames misuse as replacing learning, and declares work AI-generated or modified and passed off as one's own to be dishonest. Use not expressly permitted by the instructor is an Honor Code violation.

units.why: The same sentence lists 'thinking through ideas' as a way AI supports education, which is idea generation, so P15.
units.anchor: thinking through ideas
units.resolution_why: Found only by A; B folded it into one unit with the study-guide use. The source lists three separate supportive uses in one sentence ('thinking through ideas', 'making study guides or practice problems', 'help with understanding difficult concepts'), each a distinct permitted use, so it is kept as its own unit.

units.why: The policy names study guides and practice problems as supportive uses: 'making study guides or practice problems'. This is a permission for study aids, so P14.
units.anchor: making study guides or practice problems
units.fit_note: Sentence also lists thinking through ideas (P15) and understanding difficult concepts (P12) together.
units.resolution_why: A coded during-work/may; B coded general/informs. The passage names study guides and practice problems as ways AI supports a student's education, which endorses the use, so it is a permission for study aids (P14); the default restriction is carried by separate units.

units.why: It lists 'help with understanding difficult concepts' as a legitimate support, matching the concept-tutor type P12.
units.anchor: help with understanding difficult concepts
units.resolution_why: Found only by A (B merged it into its first unit). 'help with understanding difficult concepts' is a distinct supportive use (tutor), so it is kept.

units.why: The passage gives the reason for limits: using AI 'as a substitute for genuine engagement' undermines learning, which is the skill-building rationale P41, not a fairness rationale.
units.anchor: substitute for genuine engagement, or to circumvent the necessary intellectual challenges
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B restrict. The sentence is a rationale ('runs counter to the heart of education itself') with modality informs; the operative ban is coded in later units, so neutral.

units.why: It asks students to keep AI as a supplement, not a replacement for their own thinking: 'supplementing your education and replacing it'. Closest is P32 (student stays the primary thinker).
units.anchor: the difference between supplementing your education and replacing it
units.fit_note: A reflective prompt rather than an explicit rule that AI must not replace thinking.
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B restrict. The sentence advises students to 'think carefully about the difference between supplementing your education and replacing it', which is guidance and not itself a ban, so neutral.

units.why: States the purpose is "not to be overly punitive" but to ensure genuine engagement. Closest to the educative-response type P68, although it is stated as purpose, not procedure.
units.anchor: not to be overly punitive, but to ensure that you engage genuinely and deeply
units.fit_note: Framed as the purpose of the policy rather than a rule about responding to a particular case. / Gives the educational (non-punitive) aim of the policy but no actual educative response to misuse.
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all and phase when-misuse; B coded student and general. The sentence states the purpose of the policy ('not to be overly punitive, but to ensure that you engage genuinely') and addresses the student as 'you'; it is a principle and not a sanction step, so student/general.

units.why: The sentence acknowledges that 'you will most likely use it in your chosen field', a professional-readiness argument that AI matters for careers (P44), though it does not say courses teach it.
units.anchor: you will most likely use it in your chosen field
units.fit_note: Acknowledges AI in future careers but does not say courses teach AI use. / Only acknowledges likely use at work; does not say courses teach AI use.

units.why: AI is limited so that students 'acquire the knowledge and skills that your assignments are meant to produce'; this is the skill-building rationale, P41.
units.anchor: acquire the knowledge and skills that your assignments are meant to produce

units.why: The sentence classes passing off AI-generated or AI-modified work as one's own as 'academic dishonesty'. I chose P36 (classification as misconduct) over P19 because the sentence defines the offence rather than listing a banned use.
units.anchor: including work generated or materially modified by AI, constitutes academic dishonesty
units.resolution_why: A coded when-misuse, B general. The sentence says work generated or modified by AI and passed off as one's own 'constitutes academic dishonesty', which defines what counts as misuse, consistent with the next unit that sets the Honor Code consequence; when-misuse.

units.why: "violates an instructor's articulated policy ... will be considered a violation of the Honor Code": breaking an instructor's AI rule is classed as an Honor Code violation, so P36.
units.anchor: Use of generative AI in a way that violates an instructor’s articulated policy
units.policy: Using generative AI in a way that violates an instructor's articulated policy is a violation of the Honor Code.
units.resolution_why: Same passage and codes; B added a normalized policy because the anchor alone does not state the consequence. Kept B's policy after checking it against the source sentence.

units.why: "using it to complete coursework in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member" is a violation: when permission is absent, use is not allowed. This is the fallback rule, P06.
units.anchor: using it to complete coursework in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member
units.policy: Using generative AI to complete coursework in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member is a violation of the Honor Code.
units.resolution_why: Same codes; B added a normalized policy because the anchor alone omits the Honor Code consequence. Kept B's policy after checking it against the source.

units.why: Students with questions are directed to a named office, 'the Office of Academic Standards', i.e. human help (P72).
units.anchor: please contact the Office of Academic Standards
units.fit_note: Directs to an office for policy questions, not to instructors or writing support. / Names the office for questions about the policy; not learning support (P72).
units.resolution_why: A coded P72 course-start, B coded P115 general. The sentence ('If you have questions about this policy, please contact the Office of Academic Standards') sends students to a human office, which is P72 (P115 is for pointing to pages or documents). It is not about starting a course, so the phase is general.

documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: Statement on Generative AI and Academic Integrity (May 2023)
documents.stance_why: The statement says 'the authority to define the appropriate use ... rests with the faculty' and gives prohibit or encourage as examples, so the document sets no stance itself and delegates.
documents.summary: A May 2023 university statement that leaves AI rules to faculty, who may ban or encourage it. Instructors must communicate expectations; students must not pass off AI-generated work as their own, and violations go through the Honor Code procedures.

units.why: The statement says 'we want to embrace every available tool' and that technology 'provides new opportunities', naming benefits without setting a rule (P87).
units.anchor: we want to embrace every available tool that will aid in this educational journey
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B encourage. 'we want to embrace every available tool' is a mission-level rationale (modality informs) and states no student-facing permission, so neutral.

units.why: Replacing "the rigorous demands of and personal engagement with their coursework" with AI "runs counter to the educational mission": limit justified by learning, P41.
units.anchor: replace the rigorous demands of and personal engagement with their coursework
units.policy: When students use generative AI to replace the rigorous demands of and personal engagement with their coursework, it runs counter to the educational mission of the University.
units.resolution_why: A neutral, B restrict. The sentence is a rationale ('runs counter to the educational mission') with modality informs; the operative rule is in the units that follow, so neutral. Kept B's normalized policy.

units.why: Says AI "hold[s] promise for deploying knowledge in service to others and accelerating the discovery of new knowledge": a benefit statement, P87.
units.anchor: promise for deploying knowledge in service to others and accelerating the discovery of new knowledge
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'hold promise for deploying knowledge in service to others and accelerating the discovery of new knowledge' states a benefit of AI, which is real policy content (P87), so it is kept.

units.why: The university hands the decision to faculty: 'authority to define the appropriate use ... rests with the faculty'. That is P04.
units.anchor: the authority to define the appropriate use, study, and deployment of these technologies

units.why: Instructors 'may choose to prohibit or strictly manage' AI, e.g. in an intro writing course. It permits an instructor-set ban, so P04.
units.anchor: an instructor may choose to prohibit or strictly manage the use of these technologies
units.fit_note: Example of one option (prohibit or strictly manage); the ability to choose is the rule.
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B restrict. The sentence says an instructor 'may choose to prohibit or strictly manage' AI, which delegates the choice to the instructor and sets no stance, so neutral.

units.why: Instructors may instead 'encourage the use of these technologies as part of a creative process'; the choice is the instructor's (P04).
units.anchor: an instructor might encourage the use of these technologies as part of a creative process
units.fit_note: Example of the encouraging option; the ability to choose is the rule.
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B encourage. 'an instructor might encourage the use' delegates the choice to the instructor, so neutral.

units.why: Instructors must tell students their course expectations: 'responsibility is to communicate'. P09 (state AI expectations) fits; no syllabus is named, so a small gap.
units.anchor: the instructor's responsibility is to communicate to students the expectations for their course
units.fit_note: Does not say where (syllabus) the expectations are stated. / Does not specify the syllabus or assignment instructions as the place.

units.why: "It is the responsibility of students to conduct themselves accordingly" makes students responsible for following the course's rules, P78.
units.anchor: It is the responsibility of students to conduct themselves accordingly
units.fit_note: Does not say students must find the rules, only conduct themselves according to the expectations instructors communicate.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'It is the responsibility of students to conduct themselves accordingly' states a distinct duty (follow each course's stated expectations) in the same sentence as the next rule, so it is kept as P78.

units.why: Students must 'never' pass off work they did not produce, including AI-generated or modified work: ownership of submitted work (P29).
units.anchor: never to represent work they did not produce as their own
units.resolution_why: A coded P29, B coded P19. The words 'never to represent work they did not produce as their own' state ownership of what is submitted (P29); AI-generated work is named as an example, and P19 (do not have AI produce the work you submit) fits less well.

units.why: Misuse where AI is used "in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member" is not allowed by default, so this is the fallback rule, P06.
units.anchor: uses generative AI in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member
units.fit_note: The fallback is implied by the trigger for procedures rather than stated as a rule.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. The clause 'where a student uses generative AI in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member' repeats the default that unexpressed permission means a violation, and the sentence ties it to the Honor Code process; real policy, kept.

units.why: "the procedures and remedies outlined in the Procedural Appendix ... will be used to resolve the matter" sends violations to the formal procedure, P81.
units.anchor: the procedures and remedies outlined in the Procedural Appendix to the Honor Code
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all and modality informs; B coded admin and must. 'the procedures and remedies ... as administered by the Office of Academic Standards, will be used to resolve the matter' commits the office to a process, so admin/must.

documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: Policy Update: AI Editing Tools (Fall 2024)
documents.stance_why: The update sets no stance of its own: it says 'if your instructor prohibits the use of gen AI ... this prohibition includes the use of editing tools', extending whatever the instructor decides.
documents.summary: A Fall 2024 Honor Code update clarifying that AI editing tools such as Grammarly count as generative AI, so an instructor's prohibition covers them unless stated otherwise. It warns about detector flags and unattributed AI suggestions, and tells students to check the syllabus or ask.

units.why: Defines AI editing tools as tools that 'suggest revisions' and so produce 'AI-generated text', which sets what the policy covers (P61).
units.anchor: AI-powered editing tools like Grammarly and WordTune
units.resolution_why: A student, B all. The sentence defines AI editing tools for the reader ('suggest revisions to your writing'), and the page addresses students, so student.

units.why: A prohibition 'includes the use of editing tools', so AI proofreading is banned where AI is. P21 (no AI to proofread or check graded work) fits best.
units.anchor: this prohibition includes the use of editing tools, unless explicitly stated otherwise
units.fit_note: Scope clause: editing tools are covered by an instructor's AI prohibition unless the instructor says otherwise.

units.why: Warns that detectors flag even minimal editing-tool help; it concerns detector use (P40) but gives a warning, not a rule.
units.anchor: even a small number of suggestions from an AI editing tool
units.fit_note: Says detectors will flag editing-tool text and that this is not a false positive; it does not tell instructors to use detectors. / Warns of detector sensitivity rather than stating a rule.
units.resolution_why: Matched A's detector-flag unit with B's 'can cause it to be flagged as 100% likely'. Both said P40 with a fit note; the type is kept because AI-detection tools are named, and the notes record that the passage warns students about the flag rather than describing a detection practice.

units.why: States that when a detector flags a text edited with an AI tool, "This is not a false positive"; it speaks about how detector results are read, P40.
units.anchor: This is not a false positive, as the detector has correctly identified the AI-generated content
units.fit_note: Tells students detector flags on editing-tool text are correct; no rule on detector use.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'This is not a false positive, as the detector has correctly identified the AI-generated content' is a separate claim that a flag on editing-tool text is valid; kept with P40 and the fit note.

units.why: Using AI suggestions 'without proper attribution' is academic dishonesty: nondisclosure is the violation (P28), not just a disclosure duty (P24).
units.anchor: using AI-generated suggestions without proper attribution can be considered a form of academic dishonesty

units.why: "If you aren't sure, check the syllabus or ask your instructor for clarification": ask before using, P10.
units.anchor: If you aren’t sure, check the syllabus or ask your instructor for clarification

units.why: Students should 'consider citing the use' of permitted editing tools, a soft disclosure recommendation (P24).
units.anchor: consider citing the use of these tools if they are allowed

documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: AI Recommendations for Instructors
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors to 'be explicit with students about your expectations' and supplies sample statements from ban to 'generally acceptable', so the stance rests with instructors.
documents.summary: Honor Code office recommendations for instructors: warn students that chatbots are unreliable, state expectations in the syllabus and Canvas, and treat unauthorized use as an Honor Code violation. It offers four sample statements ranging from a ban to attributed use, and urges instructors to try the tools and discuss them.

units.why: Tells instructors to "Remind students that ChatGPT and related tools do not meet the standards normally expected of academic or professional work", then lists missing citations, non-reproducibility and "hallucinations": output reliability, P31.
units.anchor: do not meet the standards normally expected of academic or professional work
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors to tell students; lists the limits but not a duty to verify.

units.why: Names 'the lack of accountability for the ethical and equitable sourcing of information' as a known problem with the tools, an ethical concern (P53).
units.anchor: the lack of accountability for the ethical and equitable sourcing of information

units.why: Argues that critical thinking and writing are 'the hard but essential core' of the education, a skill-building reason for care with AI (P41).
units.anchor: form the hard but essential core of a liberal arts education

units.why: Instructors should 'be explicit with students about your expectations' for assignments, exams and class: communicate AI rules (P09).
units.anchor: Be explicit with students about your expectations regarding the use of ChatGPT
units.fit_note: Covers assignments, exams and classroom, not only the syllabus.

units.why: Instructors should make clear that 'unauthorized use ... will be considered a violation of the Honor Code': misconduct classification (P36).
units.anchor: unauthorized use of generative AI will be considered a violation of the Honor Code

units.why: Editing tools like Grammarly count under a prohibition: AI proofreading/revising is banned where AI is (P21).
units.anchor: This includes AI editing tools (such as Grammarly)
units.fit_note: Scope clause addressed to instructors: AI editing tools count as prohibited AI.

units.why: Instructors are advised to add 'a specific statement in your syllabus and on Canvas': syllabus AI statement (P09, as a recommendation).
units.anchor: Consider adding a specific statement in your syllabus and on Canvas

units.why: The page supplies four sample syllabus statements for instructors to adapt (P110).
units.anchor: The following sample statements may be helpful in crafting statements
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. 'The following sample statements may be helpful in crafting statements' introduces the supplied sample syllabus statements (P110), so it is a real unit and kept.

units.why: The sample statement says students 'signed the Honor Code pledge' and that this includes appropriate generative AI use; it ties the pledge to AI (P111).
units.anchor: you signed the Honor Code pledge
units.fit_note: The pledge is invoked as already signed; no new signing is required.

units.why: Sample 1: AI composition and editing tools banned 'unless it is specifically permitted for the assignment', a default ban with exceptions (P01).
units.anchor: you may not use any generative AI composition or editing tools
units.resolution_why: A coded P01 during-work, B coded P06 course-start. The sample statement bans 'any generative AI composition or editing tools, unless it is specifically permitted for the assignment', which is a default ban with assignment-level exceptions (P01); P06 (fallback when the syllabus is silent) does not describe it. The rule binds student work, so during-work.

units.why: Sample 2 says the tools 'may not be used for assignments in this course unless specifically stated in the assignment': a default ban with assignment-level exceptions, student-facing and binding work, so P01 (not the silent-syllabus fallback P06), must-not, during-work.
units.anchor: may not be used for assignments in this course unless specifically stated in the assignment
units.resolution_why: Both coders coded P06; A coded phase during-work, B course-start. 'may not be used for assignments in this course unless specifically stated in the assignment' is a default ban with exceptions, the same shape as the previous sample statement, so P01 and not the fallback type P06. The rule binds work, so during-work.

units.why: "Using these tools without my permission puts your academic integrity at risk" ties unauthorized use to integrity, P36.
units.anchor: Using these tools without my permission puts your academic integrity at risk
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'Using these tools without my permission puts your academic integrity at risk' is a distinct statement in the sample text linking unauthorized use to integrity (P36); kept.

units.why: Where AI use is permitted, content 'must be properly attributed': disclosure with the submission (P24).
units.anchor: the content generated or modified by AI must be properly attributed

units.why: Sample 3 makes AI 'generally acceptable', a permit-by-default rule (P02).
units.anchor: The use of AI tools is generally acceptable in this course
units.resolution_why: A coded during-work, B course-start. The sample says AI use 'is generally acceptable in this course', a default that binds student work, so during-work.

units.why: AI must be attributed "like any other source ... in a manner that can be reproduced by the reader": the rule is to attribute, P24.
units.anchor: must always be attributed in a manner that can be reproduced by the reader
units.fit_note: Also treats AI like any other source (P45), which the type does not capture.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'must always be attributed in a manner that can be reproduced by the reader' is the attribution rule, separate from the example of what reproducible attribution includes, so it is kept.

units.why: Gives what reproducible attribution contains: "the date accessed, the web address or URL accessed, and a description of the prompt": citation details, P25.
units.anchor: the date accessed, the web address or URL accessed, and a description of the prompt
units.resolution_why: A coded must, B informs. The sentence says 'An example of reproducible attribution includes the date accessed, the web address or URL accessed, and a description of the prompt', which illustrates the form and is not a command, so informs.

units.why: Students are 'responsible for assessing the quality, completeness, and accuracy' of AI information: verify output (P31).
units.anchor: you are responsible for assessing the quality, completeness, and accuracy
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B permit. 'you are responsible for assessing the quality, completeness, and accuracy' is a verification duty (P31) and takes no position for or against AI use, so neutral.

units.why: Sample 4: students 'will be required to describe the uses and process' where assignments allow AI, a description/reflection requirement (P26).
units.anchor: you will be required to describe the uses and process

units.why: Instructors are told to 'become familiar with ChatGPT', supporting their own learning (P63).
units.anchor: Become familiar with ChatGPT and related tools

units.why: "Engage with colleagues, students, and others in dialogue regarding the use and misuse of generative AI": faculty conversation about AI. P63 chosen over P66 because it is about colleagues and discipline, not explaining rules to students.
units.anchor: Engage with colleagues, students, and others in dialogue
units.fit_note: Also covers dialogue with colleagues and the disciplines, not only with students. / Includes students in the dialogue, which P63 does not capture.
units.resolution_why: A coded P66, B coded P63. 'Engage with colleagues, students, and others in dialogue regarding the use and misuse of generative AI' is addressed to instructors as a way to learn about AI and shape policy with a community, which is P63 (faculty communities); P66 is explaining rules to students. The fit note records the student part.

units.why: Predicts AI will be 'embedded within the common applications' students use. It is a forecast, not a rule on embedded-tool use, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: pervasive, ubiquitous, and embedded within the common applications
units.uncovered_note: Forecast that AI will become pervasive and embedded in everyday applications, offered as context for rethinking teaching. / Warns that AI will be embedded in common applications and tools students use; no rule attached.

units.why: "a vital conversation to which we invite your thoughts and advice" invites feedback on standards for teaching and integrity, P54.
units.anchor: a vital conversation to which we invite your thoughts and advice
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'a vital conversation to which we invite your thoughts and advice' invites faculty feedback on the guidance. It is the closest the page comes to a review cycle (P54); kept with a fit note.

units.why: Instructors should 'put your assignments into the system to see how it responds', testing assignments against AI; this is a way to learn the tools (P63).
units.anchor: put your assignments into the system to see how it responds
units.fit_note: Specifically about testing one's own assignments against AI. / Specific practice of testing assignments in AI, which P63 (learn AI) only partly captures.

units.why: "ChatGPT does not know whether it wrote a particular piece of text": asking ChatGPT whether it wrote a text is unreliable, so detection-by-asking should not be used, P39.
units.anchor: ChatGPT does not know whether it wrote a particular piece of text
units.fit_note: Concerns asking the chatbot itself, not detector software. / Concerns asking ChatGPT itself, not commercial detectors.
units.resolution_why: A coded should-not, B informs. 'ChatGPT does not know whether it wrote a particular piece of text' is a fact introduced by 'remember'; it does not tell instructors what not to do, so informs.

documents.title: Establishing AI Policies for Your Course (Syllabus Policy Language)
documents.stance_why: The guide offers a 'Closed/Strategic/Open framework' and tells faculty to choose one for their course ('selecting one of the following approaches'), so it lists tiers and decides nothing itself.
documents.summary: A Notre Dame Learning guide to writing syllabus AI policies at university, course and assignment levels. It presents three stances with sample wording and examples, and adds advice on cost, opt-out, privacy, accessibility and verification.

units.why: "A clear AI policy in your syllabus takes away the guesswork": the reason for stating a policy in the syllabus; nearest P09, but it is a rationale.
units.anchor: A clear AI policy in your syllabus takes away the guesswork
units.fit_note: Gives the reason for a syllabus statement rather than requiring it.
units.resolution_why: A coded should, B informs. 'A clear AI policy in your syllabus takes away the guesswork' is a rationale that states what a clear policy does and issues no instruction in that sentence, so informs.

units.why: "Everyone gets the same rules, the same opportunities, and a fair shot at success": fairness is the reason for clear rules, P95.
units.anchor: Everyone gets the same rules, the same opportunities, and a fair shot at success
units.fit_note: Fairness argument for clarity, not for limiting AI.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'Everyone gets the same rules, the same opportunities, and a fair shot at success' gives fairness as the reason for a clear policy, which is a real rationale (P95); kept.

units.why: Policies are set at three levels, university, course, assignment, and the instructor decides at the lower two: let each course and assignment set the rule (P04).
units.anchor: aligning with University guidance, setting a course-level stance, and clarifying details for each assignment
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. 'At Notre Dame, that means aligning with University guidance, setting a course-level stance, and clarifying details for each assignment' describes the three-layer design and is a separate sentence from the next unit; kept as P04.

units.why: "align your course policy with University Honor Code language, then tailor at the assignment level": policies at three levels kept coherent, P109.
units.anchor: align your course policy with University Honor Code language, then tailor at the assignment level
units.fit_note: Alignment is with the university-level Honor Code language, not with other sections or departments. / Alignment is with the university layer and assignment layer, not with colleagues.

units.why: Syllabi should 'link to the Honor Code and any campus AI guidance', pointing students to further resources (P115).
units.anchor: Link to the Honor Code and any campus AI guidance
units.resolution_why: A coded before-course, B course-start. 'Link to the Honor Code and any campus AI guidance' tells the instructor what to put in the syllabus, which is communicating expectations, so course-start.

units.why: Course level: "State your general stance and the rationale tied to learning outcomes in your syllabus": a syllabus statement, P09. The rationale tied to learning outcomes is part of the same instruction.
units.anchor: State your general stance and the rationale tied to learning outcomes in your syllabus
units.fit_note: Also asks for the rationale tied to learning outcomes (P83).
units.resolution_why: A coded before-course, B course-start. Stating a stance and rationale in the syllabus is communicating expectations, so course-start.

units.why: The rationale is to be 'tied to learning outcomes', aligning AI decisions with objectives (P83).
units.anchor: the rationale tied to learning outcomes
units.resolution_why: Found only by A (B treated the sentence as one unit). 'the rationale tied to learning outcomes' is a separate requirement from stating the stance, aligned with P83, so it is kept; phase course-start because it is stated in the syllabus.

units.why: Assignment level: "Specify what's allowed for this task (with examples), what must be cited, and the required disclosure format": per-assignment instructions, P09.
units.anchor: Specify what’s allowed for this task (with examples), what must be cited
units.fit_note: Per-assignment specification, not syllabus.
units.resolution_why: A coded before-course, B course-start. Specifying what is allowed, what must be cited and the disclosure format for each assignment is communicating expectations, so course-start.

units.why: Names a local 'Closed/Strategic/Open framework' of three stances for courses: named tiers (P05).
units.anchor: Closed/Strategic/Open framework

units.why: "Specify how particular assignments relate to your course-level policy so expectations remain clear": assignment-specific clarification of rules, P04.
units.anchor: Specify how particular assignments relate to your course-level policy
units.fit_note: Calls for assignment-level detail inside a course policy.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'Specify how particular assignments relate to your course-level policy' is a separate instruction to connect assignment rules to the course policy; kept as P04 with its fit note.

units.why: Closed model sample: AI 'may not be used for any part of this course', a total ban (P01).
units.anchor: may not be used for any part of this course
units.resolution_why: A coded during-work, B course-start. The Closed sample says AI 'may not be used for any part of this course', a ban that binds student work, so during-work.

units.why: Closed sample: using AI for "ideas, outlines, code, or prose is considered unauthorized assistance under the ND Honor Code": misconduct classification, P36.
units.anchor: is considered unauthorized assistance under the ND Honor Code
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'is considered unauthorized assistance under the ND Honor Code' ties AI use in the Closed policy to misconduct (P36); kept.

units.why: The closed sample ends 'Ask if you are unsure'; students ask the instructor (P10).
units.anchor: Ask if you are unsure

units.why: The closed example checks understanding by 'a brief oral check ... explaining one step of their reasoning' (P34).
units.anchor: a brief oral check (five minutes in office hours or Zoom)
units.fit_note: Also requires handwritten work uploaded (a format change).

units.why: Strategic sample: AI 'for brainstorming and outlining only' limits AI to a closed list of tasks (P107); brainstorming alone would be P15, but 'only' makes it a task limit.
units.anchor: for brainstorming and outlining only
units.fit_note: Also outlining and the closed list 'only' (P107).
units.resolution_why: A coded P107, B coded P15. 'You may use generative AI for brainstorming and outlining only' limits AI to listed tasks, and 'only' is the load-bearing word, so P107; P15 is the permission to brainstorm alone.

units.why: Strategic sample: "Any text included in your submission must be your original writing": submitted text is the student's own, P29.
units.anchor: Any text included in your submission must be your original writing
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. 'Any text included in your submission must be your original writing' is a separate rule in the Strategic sample, on ownership of submitted text (P29); kept.

units.why: The 'AI use' note must list 'the tool, date, prompt(s), and how you used the output': specific citation details (P25).

documents.summary: The CSE department's guide to the Honor Code, built on worked ChatGPT examples that separate consulting from copying and resources from solutions. Instructors decide what is allowed; the guide covers citation, code marking, and reporting.
